Verify Now Blog > Rev-A Bring-Up Notes Worth Writing Before You Hit “Place Order” Rev-A Bring-Up Notes Worth Writing Before You Hit “Place Order” by: Payman Parsi Nov 11,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design Tutorial PCB design Prototyping Tutorial Byline: The Board Workflow Analyst, IntelCAD Affiliation disclosure: I work with the IntelCAD.ai team on AI-assisted electronics design workflows. This piece is educational for makers ordering a first prototype. It does not claim that IntelCAD (or any AI tool) replaces Altium or KiCad, and it does not claim automated routing, RF closure, simulation sign-off, or manufacturing. Relevant link: IntelCAD Why this note exists Ordering a prototype board feels like progress. Opening a box with a board that cannot be powered safely is expensive progress. Before you upload Gerbers, write a short bring-up packet that your future self can follow at the bench—especially on a first-spin order. This is not a PCBWay process guide. It is a designer checklist that travels with the order. 1. Define “alive” in one paragraph Write what must be true on day one: Which rail comes up first, and to what voltage? Which LED, UART, or USB enumeration proves the MCU is awake? What is explicitly out of scope for rev A (radio certification, full sensor accuracy, enclosure fit)? If “alive” is undefined, every afternoon at the bench becomes improvisation. 2. Power-first smoke plan List the sequence you will follow with a current-limited supply: Visual check for shorts, tombstones, reversed electrolytics. Unprogrammed power-up at low current limit. Measure expected rails before enabling the next stage. Only then connect programmers, radios, or external loads. Write the expected current band for idle. A board that draws 10× the idle estimate is a stop condition, not a curiosity. 3. Programming and recovery For each programmable device, record: Connector, pinout, and voltage Toolchain / probe type Boot-mode straps or “bricked board” recovery steps If the fab panel includes a programming header that is hard to reach after assembly, note that in the packet now—not after the boards arrive. 4. What the fab notes should already say Your manufacturing notes should already freeze: Stackup family (or “default FR-4 1.6 mm is acceptable”) Controlled-impedance nets, if any (name the nets; do not invent ohms after layout) Finish, solder mask color, silkscreen readability for test points Assembly: which side, which parts are DNP for rev A Ambiguous fab notes become ambiguous boards. 5. A minimal instrument list Before the courier arrives, stage: Current-limited PSU Multimeter (and preferably a cheap USB scope or logic analyzer if digital bring-up matters) Correct cables and adapters ESD strap if you care about the first board Missing cables turn a one-hour bring-up into a two-day pause. 6. Pass / fail log template Keep a one-page table: • Visual: Expected: No shorts / polarity OK; Measured: _____; Pass?: _____; Notes: _____ • 3V3 idle: Expected: e.g. 3.2–3.4 V, < X mA; Measured: _____; Pass?: _____; Notes: _____ • Programmer detect: Expected: Device ID known; Measured: _____; Pass?: _____; Notes: _____ • Blink / UART: Expected: Heartbeat seen; Measured: _____; Pass?: _____; Notes: _____ Photograph the board and the meter when something fails. Memory fades; photos do not. 7. Where AI assistants help—and stop An AI assistant can help you turn a messy project chat into a structured bring-up list and remind you of rails or straps you forgot to name. Tools such as IntelCAD fit that preparation role. They do not replace your current-limited supply, your DMM, or your judgment when a rail collapses. Closing Place the order when the Gerbers are ready and the bring-up packet exists. The packet is cheap. A confused first power-up is not. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac.
